newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Budget proves a damp squip for Irish finance mkts.
newsitem.headline: Budget proves a damp squip for Irish finance mkts.

text.p: Irish financial markets showed little or no response to Ireland's 1997 budget, with dealers noting that much of it was known before Finance Minister Ruairi Quinn got up to speak at 1545 GMT on Wednesday afternoon.
"There has been no reaction in the bond market. It was virtually all leaked beforehand and most of the forecasts were much as expected," one dealer said.

He noted that Quinn set a 1997 Exchequer borrowing target of 637 million Irish pounds or 1.6 percent of GNP, slightly lower than some market forecasts, which had ranged from 585 million to 755 million punts.
"That is reasonably comforting but the Irish bond market is really keying off international events, particularly currency developments in the EMS grid," the dealer added.
"A lax budget was expected and has been priced in, pretty much since last year. The budget has been a damp squib for the bond market," he said.
By 1707 GMT, the benchmark five-year Irish bond due 2001 was at 102.95, yielding 5.68 percent compared with 103.02 before Quinn got up to speak.
Further out the curve, 10-year paper was at 110.25, to yield 6.41 percent against 110.35 earlier.
The Irish pound also took the budget in its stride and was trading at 0.9753 stg, 2.6427 and $1.6125 by 1730 GMT compared with 0.9752, 2.6450 and $1.6145 before the details.

"The budget provides a stable enough background but where sterling and mark/Irish go is as important in determining the outlook for Irish inflation and interest rates," said John Beggs, economist at AIB Group Treasury.
But he noted that Quinn's forecast of a general government deficit of 1.5 percent of GDP this year was attainable based on the government's forecasts and looked good in international terms.
Equity dealers said the budget was largely irrelevant to their market, which gained 53.52 points or 1.89 percent on the day to close at a new all-time high of 2,878.75.
Dealers said it was largely driven by a strong performance from Ireland's two leading banking stocks following AIB's announcement on Tuesday that it was buying Dauphin Deposit Corp for $1.36 billion.
AIB gained 20 pence on the day to 427 and dragged Bank of Ireland in its wake. It surged by 16 pence to 582.
But the equity market welcomed Quinn's decision to follow last year's two point cut in corporation tax with a further reduction to 36 percent from the current level of 38 percent.
